description: I’m interested in spacecraft and lunar mission planning. I’ll use NASA data to compare sunlight and direct communication with Earth at two sites near the Moon’s south pole. I’ll lead the research and interpret the results. I’m looking for teammates with mapping, data analysis, or visualization skills to build a tool that shows how the choice of landing date affects each site.
summary: We developed CTN Aerospace Moon Atlas, an interactive website in English and Turkish that helps users explore a practical question for missions to the Moon’s south pole: when can a surface team use sunlight for power and communicate directly with Earth? Near the pole, even a low ridge can block the Sun or Earth from view. Our atlas combines hourly positions from NASA’s JPL Horizons system with lunar elevation data to calculate when each is visible above the local terrain. Users can rotate a 3D Moon, compare five south polar locations, and explore the Apollo 11 landing site as a reference. By showing how a crater rim and its floor can have different visibility windows, the atlas makes the consequences of site selection clear.
details:
For November 1, 2026, our model shows that both the Sun and Earth are visible for all 24 hours from our selected point on the rim of Shackleton Crater. On the same day, neither rises above the local horizon at our selected point on the crater floor. We built CTN Aerospace Moon Atlas so students and mission design teams can explore what causes this difference and how a landing site choice affects plans for power and communications.

Users choose a date between November 1, 2026, and January 31, 2027, and compare five south polar locations with the historic Apollo 11 landing site. They can rotate a 3D Moon to find each location, then read a timeline showing when the Sun, Earth, or both are visible. Our design connects two views of the same place. The globe shows where a site sits on the Moon, while the local horizon chart reveals how a ridge can block the view at a particular time.

We combined hourly Sun and Earth positions from NASA/JPL Horizons with lunar elevation data. At each site, we calculated the terrain horizon for an observer two meters above the surface. We processed the data with Python and NumPy, cross-checked the celestial positions using NASA’s SPICE software, and built the bilingual interface with HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. WebGL powers the interactive globe. The visibility windows identify opportunities for solar power and direct Earth communication. Actual power generation also depends on panel orientation, and radio link quality depends on the antenna and ground station.
